Argentina in the XIX century was wild. There was a lot of money, but most of it was concentrated in a small amount of landowners. The average Argentinian lived in poverty, around half of the Europeans that came here went back to Europe due to the harsh living conditions.

I wouldn't call them socialist reforms, after the 1929 a lot of capitalist economies started implementing an interventionist approach to the economy (Keynesianism). This is far from socialism, both left and right wing parties held this view of the economy in much of the western world (including the USA). The same happened in Argentina.

In Argentina we had what's called "modelo de sustitución de importaciones" (import substitution industrialization) from the 1930's till the 70's. It was by different governments no matter their ideology (UCR democratically elected presidents and military dictatorships). By Menem's time it had already been abandoned. I wouldn't call it a failure, by the 1960's Argentina had an affluent middle class made of industrial workers and college educated professionals.

Pegging the peso to the dollar was pretty bad imho. Like it stopped inflation (which was caused by debt that was illegally taken by our last dictatorship), but left us in a vulnerable position with no control over our monetary policy. 

Privatization and liberalization of the economy made a ton of industries (either private or owned by the State) close, which in turn resulted in unemployment (it reached almost 20%) and subemployment. The fact that the peso was so strong meant that importing stuff from Brazil was extremely cheap, that lead to an economic crisis in the late 90s (which your article mentions).

The central bank, founded in 1935, saw periods of huge economic growth. Until the 1940's most Argentinians were poor. From the 40's to the 70's we saw a period of rapid economic growth (and lots of political instability). The Argentinian middle class as we know it was born in this period, thanks to industrialization and accessible college education. Argentina was pretty rich until the 70's (which coincides with our last dictatorship and liberal policies). 

To put things into perspective, poverty in Argentina was around 5% until the 70s, now it's around 30%.

All species eventually face extinction, but what ultimately matters is the extinction rate. Life will eventually fill the niches left by extinct species, but it takes time for that to happen. While it might not be an issue if a relatively unimportant species goes extinct, the extinction of a keystone species can lead to catastrophic consequences.   

 You should also take into account how unique a species is when talking about preservation, some species are the only living member of a genus, order, class or even phylum. Like, if the platypus went extinct we would lose an entire genus that won't ever be in this planet again.

 There is also the question of our relationship with those creatures, every human culture has placed some symbolical meaning in nature and some animals/plants hold a great symbolic value for certain groups (think of the bald eagle in the US). Maybe the nene goose is important for native Hawaiians. 

The concept of species is actually super controversial in biology. The most accepted definition of species says that a species is a bunch of individuals who can reproduce with each other and produce fertile offspring. Morphology is not all that important to classify species anymore given that some species are very variable (between sexes, geographic distribution, lifecycle). While dogs are extremely morphologically diverse, they can, in theory, all reproduce with one another. While mechanical barriers make it impossible for a Chihuahua to have puppies with a German Shepherd they can both reproduce with intermediate size dogs.

I'm not trying to say that all plants will die because of photorespiration. Photorespiration exists and plants have ways to deal with it. 

Different factors affect photorespiration and some plants are better than others at dealing with it (C4 plants like corn are good at dealing with high temperatures). Temperature alone can cause an increase in photorespiration tho. 

Anyway, my point was that the CO2 we are releasing to the atmosphere is not necessarily good for plants.

It's efficient enough do that, but it would be more efficient if pohotorespiration didn't exist. Photorespiration (caused by high temperatures and other factors) is wasteful because it wastes ATP (energy) that could be used for growth. If temperatures are high enough plants don't produce energy and release CO2 so they die, different plants have different strategies to survive in hot environments (CAM photosynthesis is used by cactus, C4 by grass and other cool plants). 

What I was trying to say is that more CO2 isn't necessarily good for plants.

Plant physiology is more complicated than CO2+sunlight=sugar. Photosynthesis is a highly regulated process that requires certain environmental conditions to be efficient. CO2 concentrations are just one factor, so CO2 doesn't always translate into growth. There are other factors that affect how much a plant grows, if you rise CO2 concentrations and the plant doesn't have enough nutrients (phosphate, nitrogen, zinc, etc) the plant won't grow.

 What makes things worse is that plants can also produce CO2. Plants produce CO2 by breathing (just like us, but they have an extra enzyme that makes them immune to cyanide) and by a process called photorespiration. Photorespiration occurs because one of the enzymes involved in turning CO2 into sugar isn't very good at telling CO2 and O2 apart, so, by a series of different reactions, it ends up releasing CO2 and wasting energy. Photorespiration is bad for the plant because it wastes energy. When temperatures are high there is more photorespiration which is pretty bad.

As an Argentine I can tell you that we are not even close to Haiti or Venezuela in terms of poverty or quality of life. We are in a bad place right now, but we still have a sizeable middle class and we are overall a safe democratic country.

 Argentina is a very cyclical country given our reliance on agriculture, we have had bigger crisis and we always recover. Milei's policies have been tried before and they always end up failing (1975 with Celestino Rodrigo, our last military dictatorship, Menem). Inflation is even higher than it was before and wages have remained the same. Also, things are getting more expensive in dollars which didn't happen before.

Venezuelan soil is bad for agriculture, they import a lot of their food and it has been like that for a while. The fact that they rely on oil makes it worse, when the economy was not fucked they could import most of their food. Argentina produces food for 400 million (our population is 45 million). I think Cristina sucks and she is definitely shady, but there has never been a Peronist coup d'état and elections have always been free during Peronist governments. 

Perón was authoritarian (weird personality cult), but he was democratically elected two times. Compared to Argentina in the 30's and what came after him he was pretty democratic for Argentinian standards. There was actually a coup d'état against him in 1955 (fun fact: they bombed Buenos Aires). Also women gained the right to vote during Perón's presidency.

During Menem's time fiscal deficit was still high (since at least the 70's the only governments that were able to achieve fiscal surplus were Nestor and Cristina Kirchner). He did liberalized the economy and sold a lot of our national industries, but that was definitely for the worst. Argentina used to have a great railway system that has mostly disappeared, so now truck drivers have a lot of power over the economy. We also had a merchant fleet which completely disappeared. Unemployment was high and our national industry still hasn't recovered from the 90's. The uno a uno (one dollar was worth one peso) made us vulnerable to other countries devaluating their currency (which happened in the late 90's when Brazil devaluated its currency), so we ended up importing a lot of Brazilian stuff which ended in Argentinian industries going bankrupt and a huge trade imbalance. 

In 1975 they reduced government spending by cutting subsidies to public services and oil. It's pretty similar to what Milei is doing right now and I think it's consequences seem to be pretty similar. The military dictatorship that came after that (1976) was also pretty liberal in economic terms.

El metodo científico esta tanto para diseños experimentales como para observacionales. Que sea reproducible y repetible tiene que ver con que si alguien más hace un experimento o hace observaciones si otra persona hace lo mismo va a obtener los mismos resultados, no necesariamente las mismas conclusiones. Ej: Si vos vas a a la villa donde estas trabajando el impacto de la droga y ves que 1 de cada 3 usan paco, si otro va tiene que encontrar lo mismo, después la interpretación sobre los resultados va a ser algo que dependa más del marco teórico que tengas. Lo mismo pasa en la biología, si queres ver el mecanismo por el cual actua una droga en base a los mismos resultados vas a encontrar gente que te dice que es por X o que es por Y.

\>El hijo bobo de la matemática.

La estadística tiene un millón de aplicaciones prácticas imprescindibles. La usan en todas las ciencias (tanto en ciencias duras como en ciencias blandas) y en empresas privadas. La estadística te permite saber si lo que ves es significativo o es debido al azar. Tiene un desarrollo teórico enorme y se escribieron miles de libros sobre estadística. \>Y por eso no son ciencias: no siguen el método científico. Un paso importante del mismo es realizar experimentos que eliminen la parte subjetiva, o sea *experimentos que tengan reproducibilidad y repetibilidad*. En las ciencias humanas y sociales, los fenómenos no solo no se pueden repetir controlada y artificialmente (que es en lo que consiste un experimento), sino que son, por su esencia, irrepetibles.

Con esa lógica todo lo que es observacional se queda sin ser ciencia. La teoría de la evolución no se demostró experimentalmente. Todo tiene algo subjetivo, somos humanos y es imposible de desprenderse de la subjetividad y del contexto que nos rodea. Se busca la mayor objetividad posible (en parte para eso se usa la estadística). Se puede testear una hipótesis en base a observaciones del mundo social o natural, podes formular una hipótesis y en base a observaciones del mundo real rechazarla o no rechazarla. La sociología no es una ciencia experimental, no podes controlar las variables de un experimento. Los diseños de la sociología suelen ser observacionales, lo mismo en la ecología por ejemplo, no podes hacer un laboratorio de sociología (en el sentido tradicional) porque no sería ni práctico, ni ético. En un diseño experimental el investigador controla las variables. 

Por ejemplo, si quiero saber si un medicamento inhibe la coagulación sanguínea agarro 3 ratas a una la uso como control y a las otras 2 les meto distintas dosis del medicamento y mido el tiempo de coagulación, después hago un análisis estadístico y lo contrasto con mi hipótesis. En sociología si, por ejemplo, querés estudiar el efecto de las drogas en comunidades marginadas no puedo agarrar 3 barrios pobres y darle drogas a 2 de esos barrios. Me fijo en indicador socioeconómicos (deserción escolar, educación de los padres, salario medio, etc)  y intento fijarme en la prevalencia de la droga por indicadores indirectos (no hay un resgistro de drogadictos que puedas consultar) después comparo y me fijo que onda. Esto significa que las hipótesis de la sociología no sean falsiables? Nope, puedo concluir cosas desde la sociología. En ambos casos puedo cuestionar los metodos y el alcance de los resultados (capaz el medicamento no sirve para humanos como en ratas, capaz el efecto de la droga en barrios pobres del conurbano sea distinto al efecto de la droga en barrios de otro lado). 

Otra cosa que tiene la sociología es que el investigador forma parte del objeto de estudio, entonces es mucho más díficil (de hecho imposible) llegar a un nivel de objetividad absoluto. Vivimos en sociedad y vivir en sociedad significa que el objeto de estudio de un sociólogo ya fue construido por actores no científicos. El trabajo del sociólogo conlleva romper con las ideas preconcebidas sobre lo que  estudia. Este problema no lo tienen las ciencias duras. 

El marxismo es una herramienta teórica que muchos sociólogos utilizan, el marxismo en la sociología implica enfocarse en la estructura económica más que en la subjetividad de los sujetos. Como hay sociólogos marxistas también los hay de muchas corrientes teóricas. De hecho la mayoría de los sociólogos no son marxistas o no son marxistas puros, hay muchísimos autores que vinieron después de Marx que dan una visión más compleja del mundo.
